title: Fukanzazengi Part 5
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett returns to Dogen's Fukanzazengi for a fifth session, reading from the bottom of page 16 to the top of page 18, where Dogen gives exact instructions for sitting and then says very little about how to meditate. Nomon brings in Taigen Dan Leighton's description of zazen as an enactment ritual, and describes how a still body retrains reactivity even while the mind races. Nomon reads Dogen's lines on practice-realization, the dragon gaining water, the shouts and whisks of Zen stories, and the claim that dull and sharp-witted students stand equal. The evening ends with paired listening on one question: how do I divide myself?

sentences.text: Last talk there was like the sell-out crowd, so I'm glad things are back to normal.
Thank you.
Thank you for coming.
So, a few forms and notes just so you know.
I heard an extra little bell ringing.
Could you hear that, or maybe only Chris could hear that?
Okay.

One of the couple of changes that result from a priest going through the final ordination called dharma transmission is that when I meet with people individually, it's a little bit of a different structure, the way you move and come into the room and stuff.
It's called duksan, which means, well, it means to meet yourself, something like that.
And it's a little different from practice discussion.
In practice discussion, the person you're meeting with comes and gets you, and you enter together and sit down together.

In duksan, and we'll explain more of these particulars later on when you need to know, but just to give you a sketch, the teacher or the person offering is already in the room, and an assistant, from the bell probably, comes and gets you.
Then you go in and make bows and sit down and have a conversation.
But in both cases there's a sort of quiet conversation together at the root of it: a conversation about practice, about what's up in your life, about zazen.
It could be you don't have anything particularly you want to talk about, but you just go and say hello and see what emerges.
So that's what that little bell was.
And the assistant's job, by the way, anybody can do.
I was realizing there's actually only two things, or three things actually, in our entire form where you need any kind of special ordination or empowerment.
Most everything that happens here, all practitioners are invited to do, their training jobs, and they're considered to be part of the mandala, part of the matrix of practice.
So ringing the bells, anybody can do it.
Just get the training and do it and sign up.
I know Talus is trying to refine his sign-up sheet systems, so we'll hear more about that later.
And being this assistant person called Jisha, who brings people back to see the teacher offering duksan, anybody can do it.
Just get the training.
Chris is going to offer the training later, she says.
All these things are good to do when you're ready, or maybe a little bit before you're ready, somewhere in there, because you learn something about your mind.
You learn something about the way the whole puzzle is put together by being in a different position than usual.
The service looks a little different from the bell side of the cushion and has a different feeling, and it's really interesting.
And yeah, you learn a lot, like: am I ringing the bells well?
Poorly?
Did I forget one?
Is it okay?
Is it not okay?
In some fundamental way there's not really any mistakes, right?
Because it's like all religion and sport.
I think religion and sport are kind of the same thing in a way, right?
It's made up, has rules, and there's teams, and it's all invented by human beings.
When you're in the middle of it, it really matters a lot, right?
From the outside it's like, yeah, all right.
From the outside it's like those guys are kind of funny.
But somehow it seems to be a deep human need, right?
Whether you play soccer or do Zen, it seems to be something we need to do.

Anyway, the three things, I think they're the only three things that you require some kind of ordination to do, are being the officiant at ceremonies, so standing in the middle, you have to be a priest to do that; offering these private meetings, which requires some empowerments; and giving a talk that has this format to it, where you bowed and chanted like that.
But anybody can give a talk actually.
We just use a different format.
Let's use a simpler format.
So that's the student talk as opposed to the dharma talk.
So anyway, just some notes.
We can endlessly refine how to do Zen, but if we got too into it, we probably wouldn't be doing Zen anymore.

So I thought tonight we would return once again, maybe for the last time for a while, we'll see, to our twelfth century, the thirteenth century, sorry, Zen ancestor Eihei Dogen, in his seminal text on meditation called Fukanzazengi, which means a universal recommendation for zazen.
If you want to look at the text, it's actually in the chant book there, but you don't have to; you can just listen.
This is part five, I think, of a series of talks on this text.
If you wrote it out on eight and a half by eleven, it'd just be two pages.
But somehow there's at least five talks' worth of material in there.
A lot of that is because the style of literature is a little different from usual expository literature.
It's deeply referential, even self-referential in some ways.
Every line invokes or directly references some other teaching, some other ancestor.
And even the actual characters that are chosen when they're written out in Japanese or Chinese, there's more than one way to say things, right?
So the characters they choose have the same kind of referential quality to them, secondary and tertiary meanings.
And we're reading this in translation and trying to make sense of it eight hundred years later, so we're probably just getting a small piece of that.
But even still, there's so much there.
I don't know how they built these little texts.
It's kind of an amazing thing.
When you're immersed in any literature, I guess you can perform miracles.
And that's true for us, too.
Part of looking at source text like this is that we don't understand all of it, and this is a little frustrating to our usual way of reading.
The same thing happens within the formality and different actions and chants we do in formal practice, too.
We don't understand all of it, and it can bother us a little bit.
So there's a certain kind of learning there, too: to be reading something you in some way don't understand, but something comes.
Something sinks in somehow, maybe bypassing the mind and entering the heart, or whatever words you want to use.

And somehow, meeting these old teachers from our twenty-first century American point of view and trying to peer into their thirteenth century Japanese world or ninth century Chinese world, there's some sort of strange, expansive quality to it, which at times is frustrating, at times is quite wondrous.
So anyway, that's a little bit why it would take so long to read two pages.
In the last talk we finished a section in there.
I don't know what page that will be on.
Can you hand me the book, please, John?
Thanks.
Last time we finished a long section, and you may have chanted this text here in the morning service, or not.

But we last week finished on the bottom of page 16, kind of the top of page 17, where Dogen goes into a surprising amount of detail about the very particular way you should hold your body, and which leg goes on top, and how you should dress, and how you should eat.
It's surprising when you hit this section of text.
It starts out talking about Buddha, and it's poetic and evocative.
And then it's like, okay, now, when you sit down, here's what I want you to do.
This level of particularity, which we often call form in Zen, is one of the unique aspects of the Zen design, and it can take a little getting used to.

To take on a particular way of walking, a particular way of sitting, a particular way of standing, a particular way of talking, and maybe even a particular way of thinking and understanding and feeling in some way, can have a lot of benefits, actually, even though it may feel a little strange at first or from time to time.
This way of formally moving around in the room has obvious benefits in terms of community harmony.
Especially, one of the forms commonly practiced is not talking, right?
So it's a lot easier for 20 or 30 people to spend a day in one room.
There's a particular way you move around the room and you're not talking, so there are some obvious benefits.
And there's a feeling as you go through the day, which you'll experiment with a little bit on the sixth, if you can come to that, of the whole community in some way becoming one body.
There's a renunciation of individuality that's liberating in some way for the individual, and it opens to allow this emerging that can happen.
So that's one aspect of all these particular forms, and why Dogen's going into all this detail about exactly how you should do this, this way, not any other way.
There's another aspect of this that's a little more subtle, which is interesting if you think about it.
One of our American lineage teachers is a fellow named Tygon Layton.

What he says is that all these forms and Zazen itself, sitting meditation itself, are really an enactment ritual, I think he picked that term, enactment ritual, that we're ritually enacting something, playacting, if you will.
And Tygon says that all these motions and this way of sitting still and upright are actually not a technique, not a technique that will help us to change or attain some particular state of mind.
But actually they're more of an expression of something.
And this is one of Dogen's main points.
So here's a paragraph from an essay by Tygon about this.
He said,
*Buddhist meditation has commonly been considered an instrumental technique,*
so instrumental means operative, it's something that does something,
*an instrumental technique which is aimed at obtaining a heightened mental or spiritual state or even as a method for inducing a dramatic enlightenment, in quotes, experience.
But in some branches of the Zen tradition, Zazen, seated Zen meditation, has been seen not as a means to attain some result, but as a ritual enactment and an expression of awakened awareness itself.

This alternate historically significant approach to Zen meditation and practice has been a ceremonial ritual expression whose transformative quality is not based on stages of attainment or meditative prowess.*
So that's interesting, huh?
Let's read that last sentence.

*This alternate significant approach to Zen meditation and practice has been, and is, a ceremonial ritual expression whose transformative quality is not based on stages of attainment or meditative prowess.*
And you'll have to dig up the essay to find out what he says it is based on.
That's as far as I copied down.
So that's another reason why a text from someone like Dogen is a little hard to read.
It's because there's a pulling the rug out from under our assumptions as we come into this, right?
We naturally assume that meditation is an instrumental technique, we all think that, and in some ways, of course, it is.
But he's saying that in our tradition it's a bigger thing than that and has something more to do with expression than attainment.
And this is echoed in our text here.
After going into all this detail about how to arrange the space and arrange the body in Fukanzazengi, he then says very little about how to meditate.
That's the other thing that's interesting.
It's interesting how much of something there is and how little of something there is when you look at a text.
You're like, why didn't they leave that out?
So that's a teaching, too.
Here we have the famous and famously confusing teaching, which is written in our translation as "Think of Not Thinking."
How do you think of not thinking?
So this is the second paragraph on page 17, the end.
Excuse me for interrupting myself so much.
*Think of not thinking.
How do you think of not thinking?
Non-thinking.
This in itself is the essential art of zazen.*
Then we move on to another topic.

And if we were writing this as a text to help us understand how to effectively employ an instrumental technique to gain something, we would probably talk a lot more about breath counting and attitudes and which are important things to talk about.
But he does not talk about that.
We're getting towards the end of the capping up of last time.

The other thing I shared last time was that when I was looking at a character-by-character translation on the Internet of this text, the characters that are translated as this little teaching about not thinking and non-thinking actually could have a different translation, quite different.
So this is a little bit secondhand scholarship.
Take this with a grain of salt, excuse me, [unclear: "but thought too"].
But here's another translation of the characters that make up that, which is quite a little bit more descriptive of how to do it.
So maybe it says,
*When a thought arises, bring it into spacious awareness.
Wake up to what is, and just then it ceases to exist.
Take plenty of time.
Forget all involvements.
The self will naturally become whole.
This is the vital art of sitting zazen.*
I'm sure that includes a little bit the next sentence too.
But the part that corresponds to thinking not thinking is just this: *When a thought arises, bring it into spacious awareness.
Wake up to what it is, and then it ceases to exist.* So yeah, it's really just those two lines.
Excuse me, I was unclear last time.
It corresponds to our confusing not thinking, non-thinking.

But even that is pretty brief, quite a bit briefer than other sections of our text, which deal with the particulars of how to enact this ritual, and also the context in which it's done, and the context in which we can think about it.
The context, which is explained more in the beginning of our text, is essentially to recognize some important things that we don't notice.
The recognition is that we are in the presence of our ancestors, in a very real way, and that when we practice the way of Buddha, Buddha is right there, right now.
There's a sense in this understanding of immediacy and a sort of inherent completion.
So Dogen actually invented a little phrase that gets translated as practice-realization.
It's not practice, then realization, or realization, then you practice more.
It's practice and realization kind of arise together.
So this is an important point, and it's a little hard for us to really get our mind around, because the mind that we try to get around things doesn't really work this way.
It works in an instrumental kind of operative way.
So we need to access a sort of bigger sense of mind.
Then he goes on and says,
*The zazen I speak of is not learning meditation.
It is simply the dharma gate of repose and bliss, the practice realization of totally culminated enlightenment.
It is the manifestation of ultimate reality.
Traps and snares can never reach it.*
So on the one hand, a lot of enthusiasm, which we can appreciate, that this is a really great way to practice.
But there are some particular points in there that are interesting, too.
Again, the same theme of completion and enlightenment arises.
Here's that practice realization in the middle, that just to sit down in this way, this very particular way, is Buddha sitting down, is already enlightenment.

And the suggestion here, what's implied, is that we pay a little less attention to our relative mental states and our thoughts and our emotions, the way that we usually understand them, and feel our way into something a little wider.
Our thoughts and desires and things we don't like and all that stuff are always in reference to a sort of separate self.
You can't really desire something unless you're over here and the something is over there.
So that sort of separation and self-reference is required for that sort of grasping mind to even exist.

And so Dogen is saying, when he says traps and snares can never reach it, this is sort of reaching outside of that place where there's stickiness and trapping and being caught by things, all that which we actually experience on a daily basis, if we're honest, pay attention.
Sometimes it's quite subtle, right, the ways that we get trapped and snared.
Sometimes it's very small, but you can see it.
It's like, oh, trapped again, the snare tightening around my noose, my neck or whatever.
But even within the context of our thinking, there are some real ways that we can work with this.
It wouldn't be that helpful to just say, well, forget about your thinking.
People do say that.

And maybe in some context, maybe in a formal meditation retreat where everything's arranged and you have a lot of trust in the organizers and you're kind of in the flow and they say, forget about your thinking.
Oh, you can for a second.
But we have our thinking.
Our thinking is constantly arising.
It's arising from our conditioned self.
We're not trying to get rid of that.
We're just trying to sense it, sort of recontextualize so we don't have to suffer.
So we don't have to suffer.
So there are ways to look at this kind of teaching of the immediacy of enlightenment and the power of enacting sort of Buddha's meditation.
It actually does kind of make sense to our limited minds.
So we should access those to help us out.
One of the ways that we can look at it from that mind, the operative mind, is we can think about the incredible power of just sitting still.
When the body is still, even if the thoughts are still raging and the emotions are turbulent, even if that's true, when there's stillness, at least two really important things can happen.
The first is just the basic fact.
This is so simple, you wouldn't even think about it.
The basic fact that we are not reacting with our body, with our voice, to the things that arise in the mind.

An urgent thought arises, oh my god, I forgot to fill in the blank, and in the context of zazen, it could be embarrassing to run out of the room to go, I don't know what, turn off your lights or something, or something even subtler, whatever, than that.
So there's just a sort of re-patterning, a re-patterning of reactivity that's incredibly transformational.
But the funny thing about it is, from the point of view of the subjective mind, you might not notice that, right?
The subjective mind says, Oh my god, here I am at the zendo.
My mind is racing, I'm worried about whether I left the lights on in the car, I'm worried about whether I remembered to call my sister back, I'm worried about what...
So the mind is still racing, and the subjective mind says, "Oh man, what a cock up this is.
I should never come back here," embarrassed to show my face.
And yet, you are Buddha.
You're sitting still, you're not jumping up to get on the phone, you're allowing these thoughts to come and go.
Whether you want to or not, they're coming and going, right?
It doesn't matter in a way what you do.
The body is sitting zazen.
Who is the me, who is the one who's running the show?
It becomes a little less clear, and maybe a little more open, and a little more liberating.
So that's really a powerful kind of repatterning.
We talk about the mind and the body as if they were separate, as a kind of convenient way to talk, but of course it's not true.
They're completely bound together, and there's all kinds of science to back me up on this.
How we think affects the body, and how the body is affects what we think, absolutely.

But to shift the, I don't want to say balance of power, but to shift the center, to shift the center, is really a powerful way to support our life, and we'll ooze into our life in all kinds of ways, inevitably, inevitably.
That cultivation of non-reactivity that just is structural ends zazen.
It doesn't matter if you're really still following your breath, or remembering all the instructions.
You stay in your seat, you're a Buddha, and you're living Buddha's life for that time.
So that's one aspect.

And the other aspect, a second aspect, which is maybe a little more subtle, but really important, they're all tied together, that becomes clear when we practice stillness, is again, even if the mind is racing, and subjectively our meditation feels like a failure, what starts to happen over time is we start to appreciate, even within that realm of what we usually call mind, even within that area that the mind is somehow looking at, and what is that exactly?
We don't know.
Even when the thoughts are racing, you start to see that the thoughts are not so monolithic.
They're not quite as powerful, and not quite as completely me, not quite as completely just your whole identity as you thought they were.
And you start to sense a possibility, or maybe a feeling that's beyond thinking.
So back to Dogen with his beyond thinking.
A sense of the thoughts coming and going, a sense of gaps between these urgent, important narratives.
A sense of something solid, something stable beneath and interpenetrating all this.
This sensibility goes by lots of names in Buddhism, and it's a specialty of Buddhism to explore this, although I think it shows up in all world religious systems.
Sometimes we call this emptiness.

This sense that between and behind and even mixed up in the middle of all kinds of arising thoughts in the relative world, there's some sort of non-thought, some sense of potential, some feeling that can't be judged or grabbed onto with our thinking.
Some broader field.
Sometimes we say the field of liberation, like a farm field.
Big space.
When we're caught only, when our whole field of view is just the relative world of thinking, it can be very narrow, you know what I mean?
It's very tight, especially when we get worked up about something very narrow.
And so this other aspect of stillness is this exploration, organically, and it comes and goes.
You don't always even notice it, but it's settling into this sense of: it isn't just this.
It's this.
It's bigger than any of this.
And having some feeling of that in the body and in the heart is also a powerful repatterning of understanding of ourself in the world, and is tremendously liberating.
And so that's the practice enlightenment again.
So maybe this is more or less what Dogen means when he says zazen is not meditation.
It's actually the gate of repose and bliss.
But it's not repose and bliss only in the relative world that we're thinking.

We might have times when we feel, "Oh, I feel blissful," and this is functional in the relative world, but it's a repose and bliss that can contain even all kinds of aversive thinking and emotions, deep misery and despair, even the worst, most difficult human emotions.
Aren't those heart emotions strange?
I mean, what are they anyway?
Are they real?
And yet they color our life so deeply and can take our life.
There's a sad story going around the Zen wires.
There's a young man, I think maybe 40 or so, a Zen student at San Francisco Zen Center, who killed himself at the center last week.
Yeah, so this is powerful stuff we're talking about.
I like to make light of thinking and emotion, but it's powerful stuff.
And even all these odds in the world might not help, so this is not a complete solution to a human life, but it's a support, it's a support.
Yeah, they're really trying to figure it out.
I didn't know this fellow particularly, but I know many people who knew him well.
It's very difficult.
It doesn't make sense, of course.
Of course it doesn't make sense.
So then anyway, Dogen goes on to again enthuse about how great this actually is.
If you can feel this, even once, even for a second, a nanosecond, he says:
*If that happens, once its heart is grasped, you are like the dragon when he gains the water, like a tiger when she enters the mountain.
For you must know that just there in Zazen, the right Dharma is manifesting itself, and that from the first, dullness and distraction are struck aside.*
So in China and Japan, dragons are water creatures, not so much in Europe, but they're the creatures of the water, and tigers are creatures of the mountains.
So the metaphor there is really coming home.
When you feel this sense of practice enlightenment, this sense of enactment of Buddha, you're really coming home.
*You must know that right there, the right Dharma is manifesting itself.* Dharma is a sort of multivariate word in Buddhism.
It has a lot of meanings.
What's interesting here is that Dharma can mean both the teachings and experience.
It means the teachings, and it means experience itself.
So the teachings and experience are, sort of, one in that moment.
And again, this bit, *from the first, dullness and distraction are struck aside*.
You can read this with your conventional way of thinking and say, you know what I mean?
Maybe everybody's thinking that when they read.
Do you think about this when you chant it?
Maybe it's too early in the morning.
When we chant it, people don't think at all.
One doesn't always think, relatively, that dullness and distraction are struck aside.
Sometimes one feels, ah, I feel really dull.
I've got to do something with my breath awareness or something.
I'm really dull and distracted.
But that's only part of the story.
That's what he's saying.
And it's not the most important part of the story.
So, a Japanese character side note.
Where it says repose and bliss, repose is the word *on*.
I wish I could have brought a big sketch of the character.
It looks like a woman sitting under a roof.
So it has a sense of safety and peacefulness.
Again, a sense of being at home.
The character is evoking that feeling again.
And it's actually the *on* that's in my name, so it was fun to see it there.
Then the character for bliss, *raku*, which also means comfort, has a quality of fun and play to it.
It's supposed to look like a drum on a stand, like playing the drum.
Oddly, I was playing the drums last night next door.
It was wonderful.
So there's a sense here of safety, fun and peace.
I think we don't always associate that with Zen.
I think it's maybe some cold, hardcore path to some other thing called awakening.
But that's not what he's saying.
Then he goes on.
*Do not arise from sitting.
Move slowly and quietly, calmly and deliberately.
Do not arise suddenly or abruptly.
In surveying the past we find that transcendence of both unenlightenment and enlightenment and dying, while either sitting or standing, have all depended entirely on the strength of zazen.*
We're towards the bottom of page 17.
That's a mouthful.
Probably not the best bit of English phraseology in the translation.
But this is again literally useful.
Take care when you get up.
Dogen says so.
Get up quietly.
Get up carefully.
Take care of the body.
I always stretch the spine a little bit.
We need to get up now, the bell rang, but we're not in a big rush.
There's a sense in this of an obligation, actually, to take care of the practice in that moment.
If we think of meditation as instrumental, blah blah blah, like Dogen said, then we would think that when meditation ends we're done with meditation.
But this is saying no.
Continue this sensibility, this care, this enactment.
Have it quiet and calm and [unclear: "deliveredness"].
And you need to do that for everybody, for the whole tradition.
Then he brings up the ancestors again, very overtly, in this passage.
In surveying the past we find the transcendence of both unenlightenment and enlightenment and dying, dependent on this.
So this is a sort of bringing up a duality.
A lot of this is about how we're self-limited by language and thinking.
The way language works is you can only have a word that makes sense if it has an opposite.
You can't have up without down.
You can't have short without tall.
You can't have me without you.
You can't have white without black, and so on.
So it's baked into the language as dividing things up, which is conventionally necessary but in some spiritual way kind of damaging.
He's saying there's a transcendence of that, a stepping out of dividing things up.
Of course, in this religious, meditative context, the biggest division we can make is enlightenment and unenlightenment, right?
Now I'm a confused human being, and there are Buddhas symbolized here and there, but somewhere there are Buddhas, but not here.
And the same with life and death.
That's why he throws in dying.
Life and death is the other big category.
You can't have life without death.
But it's the way we divide life and death, really.
What's really skillful for us, if we want to live a life of peacefulness and joy?
He's not denying, he's not saying nothing dies, you're just thinking about it funny.
Actually, I had a friend, my same rock star friend I mentioned last week, who for a while was on this kick that if he just thought about it right he would never get sick and never die.
So he's not saying that.
But he is saying there's something about the way we conventionally think about sickness and health, life and death, that deeply confuses us.
It pulls us away from our deepest sense of our human life.
And I think we all experience that.
This thing I was mentioning, this sense of an obligation, is also kind of in the characters.
Let's see if I explained it to myself well here.
I don't remember all the characters.
By sitting in zazen, I didn't make good notes about this, but somehow the characters suggest obligation and responsibility.
I didn't write it down very well.
But it's a lovely thing, though.
First we hear, I'm just here for the first night.
You're saying, I'm responsible for Buddhism now.
Not exactly, but there's a sense that we're doing this for more than just ourselves.
A sense of obligation as connection.
Obligation as taking responsibility, not as a heavy burden we have to carry.
This is a really good word.
We're jamming.
We might make it.
So then he says, in addition, and he's going to evoke different things from the tradition just to make sure you really get he means this includes everything.
He says:

*In addition the bringing about of enlightenment by the opportunity provided by a finger, a banner, a needle or a mallet and the effecting realization with the aid of a whisk, a fist, a staff or a shout cannot be fully understood by discriminative thinking.
Indeed it cannot be fully known by the practicing of supernatural powers either.
It must be deportment beyond hearing and seeing.
Is it not a principle that is prior to knowledge and perception?*
So we just wrapped over to the top of page 18, if you're reading along.
Here we're into Zen lore, and we're again evoking this kind of instrumentalism.

As you probably know, Zen stories involve various dramatic moments where the teacher shouts at the student, hits them, shakes them to try to wake them up in some way, somehow brings up something in an abrupt way, or tweaks their nose or something like that.
In those stories it seems like that action leads the student to realize something.
But he's saying it's much deeper than that, and I've always felt that way about those stories too: there's so much implied in them.

They're like shorthand for a much, much bigger training matrix involving ten or twenty years of daily zazen and all kinds of stuff, that somehow maybe has some dramatic moment but is part of a continuity, a continuum.
In the Koan study group maybe you'll study some of these cases.
But in our particular lineage family, and the way we're more or less doing things here, we will never punch you.
A couple of times I've experimented with saying something suddenly in the interview room, and it always comes off really wonky, so forget about that.
The reason is we have enough shocks and blows already.
Right?
We do not need a Zen teacher to provide that.
Our life provides that.
So what's implied here is not so much that shocking things are going to cause some awakening.

It's that if the mind is prepared through this attitudinal change that's implied in all of this, this deep attitude change, then the shocks and blows of life are not problems to solve or get rid of but are actually instruments of awakening.
They are dharma gates.
A little later he's going to bring up that phrase, dharma gates.
By the way, there's a technical word in there, h-o-s-s-u.
I thought it was pronounced hosu, but usually the u is not pronounced at the end of a romanized Japanese word, so it's pronounced hosu.
So now you know: hosu.
That's the ceremonial Zen teacher's fly whisk.
There must be some story about some Zen teacher waving his fly whisk in just the right way at just the right time to help the students.
So that's what that is, in case you've been wondering all these years.
And I have one now.
